argument_macro_structure.dominant_argument_form: Conditional assessment of an ambiguity objection to a reductio ad absurdum
argument_macro_structure.premise_explicitness: Moderately explicit; formalized with subscripts and identity claims

argumentative_quality.dialectical_reasonableness: High; considers multiple objections and responses
argumentative_quality.logical_relevance: High; all moves bear on whether ambiguity defeats the reductio
argumentative_quality.premise_acceptability: Conditional; depends on whether one accepts extensionality, endurance, or temporal parts

distinctions_drawn: Same parts at a time vs numerical identity
explicit_definitions_given: DAUP: arbitrary collections of material parts compose a material object
D-minus: the object consisting of all of Descartes's parts except one leg

dialectical_engagement.objection_handling: Systematic; distinguishes ambiguity-based objections from substantive metaphysical objections
objections_raised: Ambiguity of 'Descartes' between material organism and abstract person
Abstract Descartes cannot have a leg or lose a leg
D-minus cannot be an arbitrary part of an abstract entity
Same parts after loss does not entail identity if coincidence is allowed
Strongest ambiguity objection: incompatible criteria of identity at different stages

method_and_evidence.evidence_type: Conceptual analysis, formalization, taxonomy of possible interpretations, conditional reasoning
named_thought_experiments: Statue and lump of clay as coincident objects

philosophical_orientation.grounding: Analytic metaphysics; mereology; philosophy of persistence and identity
philosophical_orientation.sentiment: Neutral-analytic; neither defending nor attacking DAUP outright
philosophical_orientation.thematic_focus: Whether ambiguity in 'Descartes' can dissolve van Inwagen's reductio against DAUP

structural_organization.structure_type: Sectioned essay with numbered sections I-XII; formalization followed by objections and assessment

summary_of_core_decisions: The text concludes that the ambiguity objection is partly correct but ultimately too strong: it defeats equivocal formulations of van Inwagen's reductio, but it does not defeat a version with a stable material referent for 'Descartes'. The paradox then survives as a substantive problem about composition, extensionality, coincidence, and persistence.

thesis_commitment.hedging_density_in_final_paragraph: High; final assessment is explicitly conditional on how the argument is reconstructed
